7.0.0.en: After the wall of Jerusalem and its gates were completed, Nehemiah turned his attention to the service of the Temple. He appointed gatekeepers to guard the gates of the Temple, and also singers to chant the Psalms, as David had arranged in former times. After that he also appointed Levites to help the priests and to carry out all the work of the Temple.

7.1.0.en: After arranging the service of the Temple, Nehemiah began to give his attention to organizing the city of Jerusalem. He set two rulers over it. The first was Hanani, who was mentioned in (ch. 1:2) and whom Nehemiah describes as “my brother.” He was a man concerned for Jerusalem; during the captivity he used to visit it in order to look into its condition, as is clear in (ch. 1), and he also came with Nehemiah to take part in building the wall. He was a responsible man who could be relied upon, and a lover of Jerusalem, the city of God. The word “brother” means either that he was his brother according to the flesh, or that he was one of his relatives.

7.1.1.en: The other man whom Nehemiah chose to govern Jerusalem was Hananiah, whom he had tested in the command of the royal palace, and whose faithfulness and ability in administration had been shown. So he entrusted all of Jerusalem to him together with Hanani.

7.1.2.en: For God sets over much the one who is faithful in little. Hananiah was also distinguished by his fear of God, which made him careful and far from evil, and therefore Nehemiah could be at ease in entrusting the government of Jerusalem to him.

7.1.3.en: This shows Nehemiah's excellence in administration: he placed officials in every place while he himself supervised them all. The distribution of responsibilities is necessary for successful administration; moreover, if the supreme leader, Nehemiah, is absent, affairs still go on, because there is an official in every place. This is what happened when Nehemiah traveled to the capital of the empire and then returned to Jerusalem a second time, as is mentioned in (ch. 13).

7.1.4.en: Do not hold all matters in your own hand in order to please yourself, or because you doubt everyone around you. Rather, you should take care to distribute responsibilities, to encourage those who are responsible, to follow up on them, and to accept their weaknesses and make up for them. Then you will be a successful administrator and will please God.

7.2.0.en: Nehemiah, the governor of Jerusalem, gave the following orders to the administrative officials Hanani and Hananiah:

7.2.1.en: 1- That they should see for themselves that the gates of the city were shut every evening.

7.2.2.en: 2- That the gates should not be opened at dawn, as was formerly customary, but at sunrise. The purpose was that the few inhabitants of Jerusalem should have awakened and even left their houses, and movement should have begun in the city; only then would visitors and merchants enter. Thus the enemy would not seize the chance to attack the city at dawn while many were still asleep.

7.2.3.en: 3- That each one should guard the wall opposite his own house. That is, the guard over the wall, or behind the gates, was to be organized among the inhabitants of Jerusalem by turns, so that one man from each house would go out to keep watch. This was for the following reasons:

7.2.4.en: a - The number of the inhabitants of Jerusalem was still small, and new houses had not yet been built after the destruction of Jerusalem at the hands of Babylon. There were only a few old houses, in which of course only a small number of people lived.

7.2.5.en: b - The guarding of the wall opposite its own house by each family confirms the sense of responsibility and of belonging to Jerusalem; each one defends his own house with care, and so the work of guarding the whole city is made complete.

7.2.6.en: The distribution of the watch among the inhabitants did not remove the responsibility of Hanani and Hananiah, for they supervised the watch so that, if they found any negligence, they would speak to the one concerned and warn the negligent. This signifies that each person is responsible for the salvation of his own soul, yet the priests and servants warn everyone who draws away from God.

7.2.7.en: The population of Jerusalem was small, perhaps because the city was in ruins and did not encourage settlement, except for those who cared to dwell near the Temple. In addition, of the fifty thousand who returned with Zerubbabel, some of course settled in Jerusalem and others settled in the surrounding cities.

7.3.s.en: (2) The genealogies of those returning from the captivity

7.3.0.en: It is clear from this word that Nehemiah was a man of prayer. For this reason, after he had organized the guarding of the city and those responsible for it, God guided him to take care of the genealogy of those who were in Jerusalem and Judea.

7.3.2.en: This register had been made by Zerubbabel 91 years earlier, that is, in the year 536 BC, when he returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with about fifty thousand people. The register was kept in a treasury, but it differs slightly from the register of genealogy ascribed to Zerubbabel and mentioned in (Ezra 2). Why this difference?

7.3.4.en: Some persons had two names, one in the original Hebrew and the other acquired during his stay in the captivity according to the kingdom to which he was taken captive, such as Daniel, who was called Belteshazzar in Babylon.

7.3.6.en: Perhaps this is because Zerubbabel made two registers of genealogy, one made in Babylon before he traveled to Jerusalem and the other made in Jerusalem after he arrived there. The difference arose because:

7.3.7.en: Some people were registered in Babylon but changed their decision to return to Jerusalem and held fast to their possessions in the Babylonian kingdom.

7.3.8.en: Some were not written in the register but decided to return afterward, and so were written in the register made in Jerusalem.

7.3.9.en: Moreover, these two registers, one of which Ezra used and the other Nehemiah, were checked against the actual situation, and both Ezra and Nehemiah made corrections in the register of genealogy. It should be noted that there was a period of thirteen years between the return of Ezra and that of Nehemiah: Ezra returned in the year 458 BC, while Nehemiah returned in the year 445 BC. During this period some of the Jews naturally died, which is another reason for the difference between the register of genealogy mentioned here and the other register mentioned.

7.3.10.en: May you depend on prayer before every task, and even delight in prayer, because it is the means of enjoying divine love and fellowship with it. Then your heart will be at peace, for God will guide you to your good and the good of all around you.

7.3.12.en: These are those in authority among the people: the chief priests, the Levites, the singers and the gatekeepers, who will be mentioned in the following verses.

7.3.13.en: This shows Nehemiah's success in administration and his love of sharing the work with those in authority, for this leads to the success of undertakings. It also shows that Nehemiah did not monopolize authority.

7.3.15.en: Nehemiah took care to make genealogies for those who lived in Jerusalem and Judea for the following reasons:

7.3.16.en: 1- To make sure of the faith of all who were there, so as to be certain that they worshiped God faithfully.

7.3.17.en: 2- Preserving the genealogies was necessary until the coming of the awaited Christ, who would come from the tribe of Judah, as the prophecies said, and indeed from Bethlehem without doubt.

7.3.18.en: 3- To make sure of the lineage of the priests and the Levites, so that they might be dedicated to the service of the Temple, since no one else may share in this service.

7.3.19.en: 4- To know who would dwell in Jerusalem, as is clear in (ch. 11:1).

7.3.20.en: 5- So that each person might know his worth and importance. This signifies the importance of every believer, his place in the heart of God, and his membership in the Church, the Body of Christ.

7.3.21.en: 6- So that, seeing the greatness of their numbers, they might thank God for His blessing upon them.

7.3.22.en: 7- So that Nehemiah might be able to divide the work and the responsibilities among those registered in (Ezra 2).

7.4.0.en: Here Zerubbabel and his helpers are mentioned, twelve in number together with Zerubbabel, and they signify the disciples of Christ. The Nehemiah mentioned here is of course not Nehemiah the king's cupbearer, the writer of this book.

7.5.0.en: The leaders of the people: these are the names of the leaders of the people who returned from the captivity and the number of individuals belonging to them.

7.5.1.en: It is noted that three of the families of these leaders took part in building the wall. Parosh, the first of the leaders mentioned, had a son, Pedaiah, who took part in the reading of the book of the Law, besides taking part in building the wall.

7.6.0.en: Men of Judah and Benjamin: it is noted that the men of Judah returned to only four cities, namely Bethlehem, Netophah, Kirjath-jearim and Nebo, while they possessed 75 cities to which no one returned, but they remained in the captivity.

7.6.1.en: The children of the tribe of Benjamin, however, returned to 14 cities mentioned in these verses, although the tribe of Benjamin possessed 30 cities.

7.7.0.en: The priests: David had divided the priests into twenty-four courses, but none returned from the captivity except priests of only three courses, namely “the children of Jedaiah,” who was the head of the second course, the children of Immer, the head of the sixteenth course, and the children of Harim, the head of the third course, as is mentioned in (1 Chr 24:7, 14, 18). It is noted that the children of Pashur mentioned here belong to the course of Immer, that is, the sixteenth course (Jer 20:1). These three courses multiplied afterward and were divided into twenty-four courses.

7.8.0.en: The Levites, the singers and the gatekeepers: their number was small, since most of them preferred to remain in the captivity. This shows a spiritual weakness in those who should have hastened to return before others, because they were consecrated to the service of God.

7.9.0.en: The Nethinim and the children of Solomon's servants: the Nethinim were not of the children of Israel, but they joined the people of God in the days of Joshua and lived with them and shared in gathering wood and drawing water. The children of Solomon's servants likewise were not Jews, but they attached themselves to God and clung to the service of His Temple. All of these loved God so much that they left the captivity and returned to Jerusalem, and God rejoiced in them. They signify the Gentiles whom Christ received and for whose salvation He died, just like the Jews.

7.10.0.en: Those who could not prove their genealogy:

7.10.1.en: The Tirshatha: a Babylonian name meaning “the honorable one,” and the title given to the governor on behalf of the Persian kingdom. The Urim and Thummim: two stones carried by the high priest in order to know God's guidance by them; one was inscribed “yes” and the other “no,” and God would make one of them shine in order to declare His will (Num 27:21). Those who could not prove their genealogies were from the people and from the priests.

7.10.2.en: Sadly, some of the priests had married women who were not of the seed of the priests or the Levites, or even of the Jews generally, but had married foreign women. One example was a priest who married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name, and this is contrary to the Law.

7.10.3.en: The Tirshatha, who was either Zerubbabel or Nehemiah, declared that the priests who could not prove their genealogies should not take part in the priestly service, but should wait until God chose a high priest who would carry the Urim and Thummim and inquire concerning them whether they should be received into the priesthood or not.

7.11.0.en: The total number of those registered: the total number of those who returned from the captivity was 42,360 persons, in addition to 7,582 male and female servants, so that the total of men and women who returned from the captivity was about 50,000 persons.

7.11.1.en: With those who returned from the captivity there was a number of horses, mules, camels and donkeys, amounting to 8,136. These numbers are small compared with those who remained in the captivity, and this shows the weakness of faith and repentance among the Jews. Bondage did not lead them to repentance and return to God; rather, most of them were absorbed in the desires of the world and did not care to return to Jerusalem to worship God.

8.0.0.en: The Water Gate: it lies to the southeast of Jerusalem and leads to the river Gihon, which is the main source of the water that supplies Jerusalem.

8.0.1.en: After the wall was completed in the sixth month (ch. 6:15), and the guarding and the genealogies had been arranged, the whole Jewish people gathered with one heart. This was at the beginning of the seventh month, as we said about the last verse of the previous chapter, because this day is a feast well known among them, the Feast of Trumpets, also called the Feast of Shouting (Lev 23:23-25, Num 29:1-6). In this feast they would leave their work and devote themselves to the worship of God. In addition, the Jews used to keep a feast on the first of every month (Num 10:10). The gathering of the people on this feast shows that Ezra had succeeded, over the past 13 years, in teaching the people to worship God and to hold fast to the holy feasts, so that they gathered in Jerusalem of their own accord and not because anyone summoned them. They had seen the work of God and His help to them in building the wall of Jerusalem under the leadership of Nehemiah, and so they took care to come to offer holy worship to God on this feast.

8.0.2.en: The people gathered in the square in Jerusalem, before the Water Gate, because it was a large square that could hold the great numbers of the people, whom the court of the Temple could not hold.

8.0.3.en: The gathering of the people as one man shows the unity that appeared after the return from the captivity. There was no longer a kingdom of Israel and a kingdom of Judah; rather, the distress of bondage had led them to repentance and the love of God, and so they came forward with one heart to worship Him.

8.0.4.en: The gathering at the Water Gate signifies the gathering before Christ, the living water, and the Holy Spirit, the fountain of life. Christ declared of Himself that He is the water of life, and that was at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem (Jn 7:37, 38). The Water Gate lies in the east of Jerusalem, and this signifies turning toward the east in prayer, that we may stand before Christ, the fountain of life.

8.0.5.en: The people's longing for God appeared in their asking Ezra the priest and scribe to read to them the book of the Law of God. This shows the work of Ezra, and after him Nehemiah, in preparing the people, so that they became lovers of God's word and longed to hear it.

8.0.6.en: What is meant by the book of the Law is not the five books of Moses, but the people's duties toward God and toward one another, which are a part of the book of Deuteronomy and were recorded earlier in the book of Exodus.

8.1.0.en: Ezra rejoiced at the spiritual concern that was in the people and at their asking to hear the Law. So he hastened to bring the book of the Law on the Feast of Trumpets, that is, on the first day of the seventh month, to read from it to the multitudes assembled in the square, of men and women, and also the children who had grown up and become able to understand the words of God.

8.1.1.en: It is known from history that Ezra took care of all the books of the Old Testament (Ezra 7:6, 12), and so he was a student of the Scriptures, especially the book of the Law mentioned in the books of Exodus and Leviticus, a copy of which was kept in the Temple. The Law is the reason for their distinction from the Gentiles, and holding fast to it gives them the power of God which brought them back from the captivity and supported them in building the wall. Therefore they asked to hear the Law, the source of their strength.

8.1.2.en: It is noted that the high priest Joiakim the son of Jeshua the son of Jozadak, mentioned in (ch. 12:26), is not named in this religious celebration. The reason is not known. It may be because of his illness, or his slackness and negligence, especially since priests of his family had married foreign women (Ezra 10:18); or perhaps he did not appear out of humility and gave the way to Ezra the priest, who was distinguished in the study of the Law.

8.2.0.en: The people gathered in the morning at the beginning of the day, and Ezra stood and read to them from the book of the Law, most likely quietly so that they could understand the words, and he continued until midday, that is, about twelve noon. This means that he went on reading for a long time, about six hours. That shows how much the people longed to know the word of God and to carry it out.

8.2.1.en: The people listened with great attention; that is, their ears and their hearts were fixed on the words of God. This shows their love for God and their attachment to Him, contrary to their condition before the captivity, when they neglected the Law, and God allowed them the discipline of the captivity so that they would return to Him.

8.2.2.en: In proportion to your longing for God's word when you read the Holy Bible, God will reveal to you His love and His mysteries. So be diligent in reading the Holy Bible, and choose a suitable time to read in, so that you may be filled and rejoice.

8.3.0.en: Ezra taught the people to care for the feasts and to offer worship to God in them, so it was expected that they would gather on this feast, especially after their victory and their completing the building of the wall. So he prepared a large wooden pulpit, a platform wide enough for a great number to stand upon it, as is mentioned here that fourteen persons stood upon it. It is like the “lectern” found in the Church, but much larger, and it has a place for putting the Holy Bible, in addition to a large place on which the readers stand.

8.3.1.en: This is the first time the word “pulpit” is mentioned in the Holy Bible. The pulpit was raised above the ground, that is, it was ascended by a ladder, even if only a few steps, so Ezra stood upon it at a level higher than the people, as appears from (v. 5). Six persons stood at Ezra's right hand and seven at his left. Those mentioned were most likely priests, whom Ezra called upon for the following reasons:

8.3.2.en: 1- To show the people the priests' concern for the word of God, so that all the people would feel the reverence due to the Law.

8.3.3.en: 2- They most likely helped Ezra in reading the Law, that is, they took turns in the reading, because it lasted a long time, about six hours, as we mentioned.

8.3.4.en: 3- The standing and reading of these priests who helped Ezra gives them favor in the eyes of the people, and so encourages the priests to read the Law at other times, and the people receive this from them with gladness.

8.4.0.en: Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people. It was in the form of a scroll, that is, a piece of skin or paper rolled up, and he opened it, so that it became a large page, in order to begin reading from it.

8.4.1.en: When Ezra opened the book, the people felt the awe of the word of God, which they were about to hear from Ezra's mouth, and so they all stood in respect and reverence before God. This still happens today in the Church when the “Gospel” is read in the Liturgies and in all the ritual prayers.

8.5.0.en: Ezra felt that he was before God when he opened the book, so he blessed God and gave thanks on behalf of all the people, to whom He had given the grace to read and understand His words, since they were His people. It was a grace that the Gentiles did not yet know, but which at that time the people of God alone enjoyed.

8.5.1.en: When the people felt the presence of God as Ezra prayed and blessed God, all lifted up their hands, sharing with Ezra the feelings of prayer, and said “Amen, Amen,” declaring their sense of the presence of God, as Ezra did. And in deep reverence the whole people bowed down before God, declaring their submission to Him and their readiness to obey His Law.

8.5.2.en: Therefore the participation of the people in these days in the Church, when they pray, lift up their hands, say “Amen” and bow down before God, declares their response and their love toward God, for the ritual of the Church encourages the people to express their love and submission to God.

8.6.0.en: After the book was read on the pulpit, fifteen men, most likely priests, came forward, together with a number of Levites who studied and understood the Law of God, and spread out among the crowds of the people assembled in the square and did the following:

8.6.1.en: 1- They read the Law to them a second time, that is, each person stood with a group and repeated the reading to them, since perhaps their minds had wandered during the reading and they had not grasped some parts.

8.6.2.en: 2- They explained to them the meaning of the Law, that is, they read it distinctly and answered their questions, that is, they made all the people grasp God's purpose in the Law.

8.6.3.en: 3- Some of the people who returned from the captivity had had their language changed, since many Chaldean or Aramaic words had entered it, which they had learned during their stay in the captivity. Their language therefore differed greatly from the Hebrew language in which the Law was written, and so they needed a translation and an explanation of the meaning of the words of the Law.

8.6.4.en: It is understood from these two verses that the work was very well organized. The people did not move from their places, so that no commotion would arise; rather, the priests and Levites divided the people into groups, and in the midst of each group a person stood to read and explain.

8.6.5.en: (2) The people's response to the Law (vv. 9-13)

8.6.6.en: 9- And Nehemiah, which is the Tirshatha, and Ezra the priest the scribe, and the Levites that taught the people, said unto all the people, This day is holy unto the LORD your God; mourn not, nor weep. For all the people wept, when they heard the words of the law. 10- Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength. 11- So the Levites stilled all the people, saying, Hold your peace, for the day is holy; neither be ye grieved. 12- And all the people went their way to eat, and to drink, and to send portions, and to make great mirth, because they had understood the words that were declared unto them. 13- And on the second day were gathered together the chief of the fathers of all the people, the priests, and the Levites, unto Ezra the scribe, even to understand the words of the law.

8.7.0.en: The people were pricked in their heart when they heard the words of the Law. They felt their sins and their transgression of the Law of God, and knew that God had disciplined them with the captivity because of their many sins, and had helped them to build the wall because of their return to Him. So they felt their need to hold fast to all the words of the Law, and they wept much. This shows the sensitivity of the people and their repentance and return to God.

8.7.1.en: But the leaders of the people, namely Nehemiah, Ezra, the priests and the Levites, intervened and asked the people to stop weeping, because the day was a feast of the Lord, in which they ought to rejoice. Thus we find unity of mind among the leaders of the people, so that they were able to calm the crowds on this feast; for the feasts of God are an occasion for joy and there is no weeping in them, except the Day of Atonement, which is a type of the death of Christ the Redeemer, and so they used to weep in it (Lev 23:27). It corresponds to Good Friday in the Church of the New Testament.

8.8.0.en: The substance of what the leaders, Nehemiah and Ezra, said to the people is as follows:

8.8.1.en: 1- That they should rejoice before God, eat and drink, and thank Him for all His works with them.

8.8.2.en: 2- That they should not forget giving to the needy, who are unable to prepare food for themselves, so that all may share in the joy of the feast. This is what is meant by sending portions to those for whom nothing is prepared, for so it was customary in the feasts of the Lord, and still is today.

8.8.3.en: 3- That they should remember that the day is a holy feast to God and not a time for weeping, but for positive action, which is prayer and helping the needy, as we mentioned.

8.8.4.en: 4- They showed them that joy in the Lord gives them strength, so that they would not fear their enemies, but would go forward in holding fast to the Law of God and in every positive work.

8.8.5.en: Thank God for His gifts, and rejoice in all the feasts of God and on Sunday, and share the joy with others by helping the needy, encouraging the weak and inviting those far away to the Church.

8.9.0.en: The Levites, meaning the priests and all the understanding Levites who helped them, assisted Nehemiah and Ezra in calling the people to stop weeping and rejoice in the feast, with all the details mentioned in the preceding verse.

8.9.1.en: Even today the servants have a great part in the ministry, for they help the bishops and the priests in leading the people along the spiritual way.

8.9.2.en: And the people obeyed the teachings of their spiritual leaders in all that they said, and this shows the spirituality of the people and the extent of their submission to God.

8.10.0.en: All departed on that day, but on the following day the heads of the people, the priests and the Levites returned and gathered to Ezra in submission, to learn from him details of the Law, and perhaps they concerned the Feast of Tabernacles, which is spoken of in the following verses. This shows that the teacher must go on learning humbly throughout his life, and then God works in him with power. It also shows the great spiritual standing of Ezra, for he was the authority in understanding the Law of God.

8.10.1.en: Likewise the return of the heads and the priests to Ezra shows that whoever loves the word of God and is attached to it longs for more. The more a person reads the words of God, the more he wishes to know than others, and God reveals to him new depths in knowing Him. So after they had spent a whole day in reading the Law of God, their hearts were moved, and on the next day they longed to know more from Ezra.

8.10.3.en: 14- And they found written in the law which the LORD had commanded by Moses, that the children of Israel should dwell in booths in the feast of the seventh month: 15- And that they should publish and proclaim in all their cities, and in Jerusalem, saying, Go forth unto the mount, and fetch olive branches, and pine branches, and myrtle branches, and palm branches, and branches of thick trees, to make booths, as it is written. 16- So the people went forth, and brought them, and made themselves booths, every one upon the roof of his house, and in their courts, and in the courts of the house of God, and in the street of the water gate, and in the street of the gate of Ephraim.

8.10.4.en: 17- And all the congregation of them that were come again out of the captivity made booths, and sat under the booths: for since the days of Jeshua the son of Nun unto that day had not the children of Israel done so. And there was very great gladness. 18- Also day by day, from the first day unto the last day, he read in the book of the law of God. And they kept the feast seven days; and on the eighth day was a solemn assembly, according unto the manner.

8.11.0.en: When they read the book of the Law, they found that they ought to keep a feast in the seventh month, the Feast of Tabernacles. So searching in the word of God teaches a person how to worship Him.

8.11.1.en: The Jews had seven feasts, which are:

8.11.8.en: 7- The Feast of Tabernacles. There were three great feasts at which all the men had to come to Jerusalem to stand before the Temple of God, namely the feasts of the Passover, Pentecost and the Harvest.

8.11.9.en: It is noted that the last three feasts are celebrated in the seventh month: Trumpets on the first day, Atonement on the tenth day, and Tabernacles from the fifteenth day to the twenty-second. The Feast of Tabernacles coincides with the time of gathering the summer harvests, and so it is a day of joy in the Lord and His blessings and gifts.

8.11.10.en: In the Feast of Tabernacles all the Jews go out from their dwellings and set up booths, that is, huts or shelters, for seven days, and on the eighth day there is a solemn assembly. This is for the following reasons:

8.11.11.en: 1- To remember the days of their sojourning in the wilderness of Sinai, so that they live in the spirit of being strangers to the world and do not cling to the material things and goods of the land of Canaan.

8.11.12.en: 2- So that they might feel unity, since the rich and the poor all live in booths which they make on the roofs of their houses or in the squares.

8.11.13.en: 3- So that the rich might feel for the poor and their needs, and help them.

8.12.0.en: Myrtle: a fragrant evergreen tree, small in size.

8.12.2.en: The Law commanded the people to go out to the mountain and gather branches of various trees, in order to make their booths with them.

8.13.0.en: The Gate of Ephraim: it is in the western wall of the city of Jerusalem.

8.13.1.en: The people obeyed the word of God and made the booths, whether on the roofs of their houses, or in the courts of the Temple and the wide squares of Jerusalem, such as the square of the Water Gate and the square of Ephraim.

8.14.0.en: The people kept the Feast of Tabernacles with all exactness, and the like had not been done since the days of Joshua the son of Nun. For the keeping of the Feast of Tabernacles in the days of Solomon (1 Kgs 8:65, 66) and in the days of Ezra (Ezra 3:4), despite its greatness, was not as exact as what they did in the days of Nehemiah. In the days of Solomon the feast was great, but they did not hold a solemn assembly on the eighth day.

8.14.1.en: The people rejoiced greatly at carrying out the word of God. When they repented of their sins and wept, they rejoiced and ate, and then remembered their being strangers to the world through the Feast of Tabernacles. Such is the effect of listening to the word of God and submitting to it.

8.15.0.en: Ezra, the priests and the Levites took care, in this Feast of Tabernacles, to read from the book of the Law every day, for the people who dwelt in the booths came every morning before the Temple of God and listened to the book of the Law.

8.15.1.en: Remember that you are a stranger in the world, so that you are not occupied with love of possessions, are not troubled by any loss, are forgiving toward others, and think of eternity, and so live with God in good fellowship.

8.15.2.en: Fasting and the prayer of praise: on the Feast of Trumpets, on the first day of the seventh month, sorrow was mingled with joy (ch. 8), when the people wept at hearing the book of the Law, and Nehemiah and Ezra called them to rejoice on this great day. After the celebration of the Feast of Tabernacles from the fifteenth to the twenty-second day of the seventh month, they returned to their houses, and then came back on the twenty-fourth day to gather and offer repentance with sorrow, and then joy in praising God.

8.15.3.en: In the ninth chapter of this book we find a prayer that includes repentance and praise, as we find the same meaning in the ninth chapter of both the books of Ezra and Daniel.
